div.head: General transcription practices
div.p: Most of Joyce’s letters appear to have been written hastily. Misspellings, missing words, and irregular punctuation are common, and authorial corrections are rare. For a period from 1929 through 1931 Joyce tried his hand at typing: several of these letters include the proud or cautionary announcement “I typed this myself”.

Overall, James Joyce’s Correspondence aims for a reading text that takes into account but does not attempt to replicate details and structures normally noted in a diplomatic transcription. Reproductions of postcards and other illustrative matter supplement the reading text when necessary. Most of the transcriptions reproduce entire documents, but in some cases only partial transcriptions are provided. Sometimes, due to pieces missing from a repository collection or the presence in an auction catalog of only a portion of a letter, only fragments may have been available for transcription. In other cases, the edition’s transcription may reproduce only the unpublished portions of an otherwise published item. In these cases, a brief excerpt from the published letter is provided to indicate the context of the missing section and signalled by a brief note.
div.head: Physical format
div.p: The edition identifies the general physical formats of each item of correspondence, defined by the items themselves and also by additional information accompanying the item. The abbreviation “S” indicates the presence of Joyce’s signature, “I” indicates Joyce’s initials, and the lack of either indicates that no such self-identification is present. The term “(frag.)” added to an abbreviation indicates that part of the piece of correspondence was not available for transcription. This situation could have been due to the absence of a page or a portion of a page or the availability to the transcribers of only a portion of an image of the original. Abbreviations on envelopes (i.e. SM, SRM, SPRM) that were not sent through the postal services are noted. A full list of abbreviations used to describe the physical format of pieces of correspondence included in the edition can be found here.
div.head: Orthography
div.p: Joyce’s idiosyncratic spelling, capitalization, and abbreviation are preserved. This practice includes abbreviations without punctuation (e.g. wd, cd, yrs), contractions written without an apostrophe, and varying presentations of superscripts. Joyce’s spelling generally conforms to British practice, though sometimes follows American practice. The edition provides Joyce’s text. Joyce’s use or omission of diacritics is followed precisely. When erroneous usage might cause confusion on the part of a reader of the transcription, a corrected spelling is provided in a box under the designation “for”; if further explanation is required, a note is provided. Joyce’s writing of ampersands varies; these have all been standardized to “&”. Joyce’s practice of indicating the titles of works is inconsistent. Sometimes he underscores individual words, sometimes he underscores a string of words, sometimes he omits underscoring. In all cases, the transcriptions follow Joyce’s practice as accurately as possible and render Joyce’s underscoring as underscores, not as italics. When this practice might cause confusion, a note is provided.
div.head: Dates
div.p: Dates assigned by Joyce to letters and cards are always transcribed in the form given, including the mixing of Roman and Arabic numerals, slashes, and periods. Humorous or commemorative dates (“Easter Eve” etc.) are always given as written by Joyce. The metadata displayed in a transcription’s header standardizes and explains all letter dates. The date assigned to a telegram in the edition is the date of transmission, when that date is available. If the transmission date is not available, the receipt date is assigned.

Information regarding undated or incompletely dated letters and cards is given in the notes. Dates of writing are established or approximated using a variety of evidence. The presence of a postmarked envelope, if clearly associated with a given letter, may be used to establish a posting date, which, in the absence of a date on the accompanying letter, the editors then assume as equivalent to the date of composition. Events or publications mentioned by Joyce in the text of a piece of correspondence, or places from which Joyce wrote that are noted at the top of a page, can be used to establish a date quite closely or even specifically. Joyce frequently repeated information written at more or less the same time to several correspondents; if one of these items was dated, the dates of others with similar information may be inferred. If a precise date of composition cannot be established, an approximate date is provided. These approximations might be based upon the establishment of a sequence of back-and-forth correspondence that contextualizes the letter in question. A letter or postcard written in green ink would indicate that it was probably written after 1938, when Joyce began to write almost exclusively in that colour. On occasion, the letterhead of a sheet of correspondence or the illustration on a postcard might be used to establish a date; however, since the compilers have noted occasions in which Joyce used stationery or postcards from a previous location, these are not always definitive identifications of places or dates of composition.
div.head: Places
div.p: Establishing places of composition is related to establishing dates of composition. Joyce was not always precise in his identification of place, sometimes providing complete addresses, more frequently writing abbreviated addresses, simply indicating the name of the city, or failing to identify a place. Identification of places may be via the postmark (though in some instances Joyce has seemed to delay mailing a letter or card while en route from one place to another), or by evidence in the text of a card or letter. The pitfalls of relying upon letterhead or postcard illustrations are the same as in the case of date identification: Joyce may not have written from the place identified on the paper used for the written text. There were some cases of intentional deception during the 1930s, when Lucia Joyce was institutionalized, and Joyce, writing from another country, asked friends to mail correspondence to her to give the impression that he was not far from her.
div.head: Punctuation
div.p: Transcriptions reproduce Joyce’s punctuation precisely, whether grammatically correct or not. Joyce’s usage generally, but not consistently, conforms to British practice – e.g. a quoted sentence’s terminal full stop would follow a quotation mark rather than (in American usage) precede it. Relatively minor errors, such as omission of a full stop at the end of a sentence, are silently corrected when they are unlikely to cause confusion. When necessary to ensure clarity, they are corrected and marked as an editorial intervention. Underlinings, especially of titles of periodicals, reproduce Joyce’s writing. A continual underline (e.g. The Dial) is differentiated from broken underlining (e.g. The Dial). Ellipses are transcribed exactly as written by Joyce. Hyphens and dashes have been standardized according to their use as follows:

list.item: hyphen (-): used in compound words as well as for date or page ranges
en dash with space on either side ( – ): used to represent dashes of whatever length in Joyce’s hand or in the annotations as alternatives to parentheses, colons, or commas

div.head: Languages
div.p: Although a single language generally dominates in a piece of correspondence (the exception being those letters written in the 1930s to George and Helen Joyce in which Joyce may alternate lines in English and Italian), Joyce frequently intersperses the main language with words in other languages. These have not been highlighted by the editors in italics or by other typographical means, but have been translated via notes into the item’s dominant language.
div.head: Names
div.p: Not infrequently Joyce misspells names either mentioned in the text of the letter or even in the salutation. Transcriptions give names as Joyce wrote them. Misspelled names that are unlikely to cause confusion are corrected in a pop-up box with reference to the edition’s standardized name format. Names intentionally misspelled as puns or jokes or whose misspelling might confuse readers are given verbatim with explanatory notes. Names that changed during Joyce’s letter-writing life (e.g. Giorgio/George, Schmitz/Svevo) are transcribed as written by Joyce; references in the notes are given to a standardized form.
div.head: Uncertain readings
div.p: Joyce’s handwriting deteriorated from being reasonably legible in his earlier years to challenging in his thirties to sometimes nearly incomprehensible in his later years. When the editors have been unable to transcribe with certainty, a reasoned guess regarding the word or passage is provided and marked as such. Illegibility resulting from physical conditions such as damaged paper or typewritten text appearing to extend beyond the paper margin is explained in a note.
div.head: Authorial emendations and interlineal additions
div.p: Overtyping, whether by Joyce or by an amanuensis, to correct a simple misspelling is not noted. In contrast, the few handwritten corrections are noted. The rare interlineal additions are included in the transcriptions with notes giving details relating to original text and to form and placement of corrections. Non-standard spacing is noted only when it affects sense. Joyce frequently interrupts continuous handwriting at a syllable break within a word. Such words are considered as being continuous unless their meaning is ambiguous. Stray marks that cannot be associated with handwritten words are not noted. Postscripts and notes written in the margins are given as part of the continuous text and described in a note if needed.
div.head: Closing and signatures
div.p: Joyce’s closing lines and signatures are transcribed precisely as written. Capitalization is given as written. Since the phrases “sincerely yours” and “kind regards” are the most frequent way in which Joyce closes, these phrases have been editorially standardized in lower-case letters. Transcriptions place postscripts signalled by Joyce by “P.S.” at the ends of letters, regardless of their place on the original page, with a note, if necessary, indicating original placement.
div.head: Typographical arrangement
div.p: Line breaks and page breaks are not noted, and no attempt has been made to reproduce Joyce’s left margin, which typically slants from the left at the top of the page toward the center at the bottom. Opening information – the place from which Joyce wrote, the date of the correspondence, and the salutation and address, is placed uniformly flush left at the beginning of the letter or postcard. Such elements are transcribed precisely as in the originals. This frequently results in variations, particularly of place names, e.g. “Paris” versus “192 rue de Grenelle, Passy, Paris”. Placement of dates of letters either at the beginning or end follows the original text, but in the transcriptions these dates are always located at the left margin. Treatment of postcards, though the writing may fill up the available space in a variety of ways, follows these practices. Paragraph indentation is standardized.
